name: {fmt}
workload: Converting each of a 1.7M-value pool of random doubles (reduced to 1-17 significant digits) to a shortest round-trip decimal string via fmt::format_to with compile-time format strings, measured with Google Benchmark; mean time per conversion.
claimed_speedup: 20.214x faster than sprintf per double (36.84ns vs 744.72ns); ~24x faster than ostringstream (885.30ns) (derived from page data); fmt README separately states '{fmt} can be tens of percent to 20-30x faster than sprintf and iostreams, especially for numeric formatting'
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102); CMake default Release build type (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for optimized code; exact -O flag not printed in the results table itself)
stars_or_usage: 25.8k stars; used in FoundationDB, Ceph, ClickHouse, Envoy, Battle.net, and the reference implementation basis for C++20 std::format
tradeoffs: Adds a header-only or compiled dependency vs. printf; compiles noticeably slower than raw printf (5.1s vs 1.6s for the bloat-test suite) though far faster than IOStreams (25.5s); template-heavy formatting machinery can grow binary size if many format-string/type combinations are instantiated; requires C++11+.
caveats: The exact numbers come from the fmtlib/dtoa-benchmark repo (linked from the fmt README's Performance section) rather than being pasted directly into the fmt README; the fmt README's own separate compile-time table (Apple M5 Max, Apple Clang 21.0.0, -O3) shows a different comparison (compile time/binary size, not speed) so was not used here. Single-hardware-sample (Apple M1 Pro) result; 'Release' build config was confirmed by reading CMakeLists.txt rather than being printed alongside the results table.

name: fast_float
workload: Parsing 64-bit IEEE-754 floating point numbers with fast_float::from_chars vs. the system strtod (glibc, default locale) over three datasets - a 111k-line real-world 'canada' JSON coordinate corpus, synthetic uniform floats in [0,1), and synthetic 32-bit integers - run single-threaded on four different CPU architectures (millions of floats/sec).
claimed_speedup: 'Three to five times faster than the strtod function available in the GNU standard library... often more than twice as fast as the state-of-the-art abseil library' (verbatim from paper Section 12); e.g. Table 9, Intel Skylake, canada dataset: 45 Mfloat/s (fast_float) vs 9.0 Mfloat/s (strtod) = 5x (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 10.2, full optimization (-O3 -DNDEBUG), single-threaded, run inside a privileged Ubuntu 20.10 Docker container on Linux
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake x64, 3.7GHz effective); also tested on AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen2 x64, 3.39GHz), an Ampere ARM server (Skylark aarch64, 3.2GHz), and IBM POWER9 (ppc64le, 3.77GHz) - see Table 8/9 of the paper
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; part of GCC 12's std::from_chars, and used in Chromium, WebKit/Safari, MySQL, DuckDB, Boost JSON, Blender, Apache Arrow, Google Jsonnet, ClickHouse
tradeoffs: Only supports float/double (and, with recent extensions, fixed-width float16/32/64/bfloat16) and integer types, not long double; header-only by design so adds compile-time/include overhead vs a plain libc call; locale-independent by default (needs from_chars_advanced for locale-style decimal separators).
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (Daniel Lemire, Software: Practice and Experience 51(8), 2021); benchmark code is published separately at github.com/lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark (git tag v0.1.0) and github.com/fastfloat/fast_float, both opened this session. Comparison is against glibc's strtod specifically (GCC/Linux did not yet ship std::from_chars for floats at time of writing), not against libc++ or MSVC STL implementations, so Windows/macOS ratios may differ.

name: Dragonbox
workload: Converting each of a 1.7M-value pool of random doubles (reduced to 1-17 significant digits) to a shortest round-trip decimal string via jkj::dragonbox::to_chars_n (full cache table) vs. std::to_chars, measured with Google Benchmark; mean time per conversion.
claimed_speedup: 1.77x faster than std::to_chars per double (28.95ns vs 51.35ns; derived from page data); also 25.723x faster than sprintf (744.72ns), directly stated in the same table
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102); CMake default Release build type (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for optimized code; exact -O flag not printed in the results table itself)
stars_or_usage: 818 stars; algorithm is used internally by {fmt} and (via fmt) by many downstream projects for double-to-string conversion
tradeoffs: Always produces the shortest round-trip representation in scientific-notation form (e.g. 0.1 -> 1E-1), not fixed-point %f-style output, so callers need extra formatting logic for printf-like output; the library's policy-based template API can cause binary bloat if many policy combinations are instantiated; header for the core algorithm is separate from the to_chars string-generation layer.
caveats: Dragonbox's own README benchmarks Grisu-Exact, Ryu and Schubfach, not std::to_chars/printf/strtod directly, so it does not by itself satisfy the WHAT COUNTS rule; this record instead relies on the independent, third-party fmtlib/dtoa-benchmark suite which does include a to_chars column. The to_chars-relative ratio is derived (both numbers are on the page, ratio computed here); single-hardware-sample (Apple M1 Pro); 'Release' build config confirmed via CMakeLists.txt rather than printed alongside the results. Last commit is just over 12 months old, hence 'stale' rather than 'active'.

name: Ryu
workload: Converting each of a 1.7M-value pool of random doubles (reduced to 1-17 significant digits) to a shortest round-trip decimal string via Ryu's d2s_buffered vs. C sprintf("%.17g", value), measured with Google Benchmark; mean time per conversion.
claimed_speedup: 16.164x faster than sprintf per double (46.07ns vs 744.72ns), directly stated in the benchmark table
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102); CMake default Release build type (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for optimized code; exact -O flag not printed in the results table itself)
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars; ported to Rust (dtolnay/ryu), Go, Julia (in the Julia standard library), Zig, C#, D, Scala, Erlang/OTP, Haskell bytestring; algorithm published in peer-reviewed PLDI'18 and OOPSLA'19 papers
tradeoffs: C implementation (plus a Java port); the highly optimized paths only cover 32/64-bit float/double, with a slower generic 128-bit fallback for long double/__float128; Ryu Printf only implements %f/%e precision formatting, not the full printf flag set.
caveats: Ryu's own README claims larger wins (15x-24x) for Ryu Printf vs. various platform libc printf implementations (glibc, musl, MSVC, Apple libc), but states no CPU model, only OS/libc versions, so that first-party claim is Tier C on its own. This record instead cites the independent, reproducible fmtlib/dtoa-benchmark comparison (compiler+hardware stated) against C sprintf, which shows a smaller but still large (16.164x) win. Single-hardware-sample (Apple M1 Pro); 'Release' build config confirmed via CMakeLists.txt rather than printed alongside the results.
